storm.summary_layperson: No storm risk this evening — skies are mostly sunny and radar is clear, so there's nothing for the Sound's usual protective effect to blunt.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Air and water are nearly the same temperature tonight (0.7°F gap, already below the 5°F buffer threshold) — the marine layer is negligible and fades further, not stronger, through the evening.
storm.detail_html:
It's a quiet evening regionally: mostly sunny, CAPE reading 0 J/kg, no NWS watches or warnings active, and the KOKX radar scan shows no storm cells anywhere in range. There is nothing approaching to evaluate tonight.

The cove's usual trick is a cool-water marine layer — a stable air pocket that sits over the Sound because the water holds its temperature while inland air heats up, and that gap can choke off incoming convection before it reaches shore. Tonight that gap isn't there: the Sound is 74.5°F and the air is only 75.2°F, a 0.7°F difference that's already under the ~5°F threshold needed for a meaningful buffer. The projection actually goes negative by evening (air cooling below water temperature, around a -4.7°F gap near 7 PM), so there's no protective layer building at any point in this window.

Because nothing is on radar or in the forecast, this modifier is moot for tonight — there's simply no storm for it to act on. If anything unexpected develops later, don't expect the cove's usual buffer; treat it the same as any inland town nearby.

What would change the call: new convective development showing up on radar, an updated Area Forecast Discussion citing rising instability, or the current 0 J/kg CAPE reading climbing meaningfully.

wind.tactics_blurb: No sea breeze tonight and the gradient itself is fading — expect a light, wandering NW-ish flow easing toward drifter conditions by sunset. Favor the center of the course and be patient between puffs rather than committing to a side.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
The air-water temperature difference (deltaT) is only 0.7°F tonight, far below the roughly 5°F gap needed to drive a sea breeze, and the station network confirms it: only 15% of coastal stations are even reading onshore. This is a gradient-only evening with no thermal driver at all. The gradient itself is weak — the authoritative station average (airport-grade anemometers) sits at 7.9 kt, right at the light-wind cutoff — and the model trend confirms it's fading, not building: forecast wind drops from around 6-7 kt now to under 4 kt by 7 PM.

Direction is wandering rather than settling on one axis. The model's own four-hour sequence swings NW → NW → WNW → NNW, and the wider station network's direction agreement is only 0.54 (a coherent wind field reads 0.8 or higher) — different parts of the region are pointed different ways. Current cove obs (RYC, NW at 320°, gusting to 15) run about a dozen degrees off the western-Sound station median (NNW 331°), which is just the normal looseness of a light gradient day, not a boundary passing through.

This flow comes in from the NW quadrant — over land, off the Belle Haven/Field Point side — so expect it puffy and shifty rather than clean. The more reliable average pressure tends to sit toward the center of the course, away from the lee of either shore. With wind this light, though, patience between puffs matters more than exact positioning.

The model only has confident output through 7 PM tonight (later forecast hours had fetch gaps); the 8-10 PM rows above are extrapolated from the established fading trend rather than pulled from fresh model data, so treat that stretch as a directional estimate.

For racers: 6 kt easing to 3-4 kt by evening is drifter territory for most one-design fleets — a light-air, patience-required race, with a real chance it goes fully variable after sunset (7:09 PM) as the already-weak gradient loses its daytime mixing.

data_caveats: HRRR forecast hours beyond 7 PM local (f05-f12) were unavailable this cycle; the 8-10 PM wind rows are extrapolated from the established trend, not model output.
